source.title: Data Scaling for Navigation in Unknown Environments
source.authors: Lauri Suomela; Naoki Takahata; Sasanka Kuruppu Arachchige; Harry Edelman; J. Kämäräinen

record.tranche_reason: Extends data-scaling analysis to imitation-learned robot navigation and reports how navigation failures vary with training-location diversity. It does not test language-model loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper's results concern real-world navigation success and failure, not held-out cross-entropy loss or language models. Its own scaling results are included as an extension to V5; comparisons of policy architectures and zero-shot performance versus in-domain policies do not test the listed scaling versions. The paper cites Kaplan et al. for power-law scaling, but the cited results are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power law of real-robot navigation failure rate against the number of distinct training locations, a proxy for data diversity. It does not measure held-out loss. Its x-axis is not parameters, tokens or compute. It studies no language model. Scaling data quantity, the analogue of tokens, saturates in its success-rate measure. So none of V1–V7 is tested as stated, and the diversity power law is recorded under fits_no_version. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation for the fitted form.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct but incomplete. The authors also conclude three things. Large-scale diverse data enables zero-shot navigation in unseen environments, near policies with in-domain data and better than in-domain-only policies. Doubling locations cuts failures about 15%. With noisy crowd-sourced data, simple regression MLP-BC policies beat generative and sequence-based architectures.
record.recipe_differences: Studies imitation-learned, map-free visual robot navigation using real-world navigation success and failure, rather than language-model pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with training-location composition and data quality: the 8-location subset causes a failure-rate dip associated with spinning loops in Kisumu. Increasing data per fixed set of locations has negligible effect.

fits_no_version.finding: Real-world navigation failure rate falls as a power law in the number of distinct training locations. The exponent is about −0.229 at 128 h total, i.e. about 15% fewer failures per doubling. Adding data from fixed locations saturates by about 2 h per location.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In imitation-learned robot navigation, downstream failure rate scales as a power law in training-data diversity (number of locations), while scaling data quantity from fixed locations saturates.

record.problems: The study evaluates only 4 test environments in 4 countries; the authors say a test set an order of magnitude larger would help confirm validity. The power-law fit results are presented in figures, and numerical fit coefficients and correlation values are not stated in the text. Data quality varies across locations.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports trends across 21 policies in Figures 7–9, but does not provide individual numerical results in the text; these are represented by aggregate rows rather than extracted policy-by-policy values. The architecture comparison in Figure 11 and the zero-shot/in-domain comparisons in Figures 4–6 do not measure the scaling relation in the listed versions.

untested.parts: No language-model loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs.
Architectures are compared on success rate at fixed data, not on loss at fixed parameter count. Not language models.
No loss-based power law in parameters, tokens or compute for a non-text regime. Only a success/failure metric against data diversity and per-location quantity.
No relation between downstream performance and model scale or pretraining loss.
No analysis of fitting or setup choices on exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. The rows measure task success/failure against data diversity in robotics, which is a related but different construct from the loss power law in V5. Evaluation covers only 4 test environments with 3 repetitions. Location counts span at most about 64, under two orders of magnitude.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Architecture effects on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.

The study tests a power-law relationship for navigation failures against training-location count, but not cross-entropy loss, other modalities such as image or video generation, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting and setup choices.

rows.subject: MLP-BC policies trained on data subsets (aggregate trend)
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of training locations while holding total training data fixed; fit failure rate against location count.
rows.measure: Navigation failure rate versus number of training locations
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports a power-law relationship and says doubling the number of locations decreases failures by approximately 15%.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for the fit or 15% estimate
rows.note: The text reports high Pearson correlation for the log-log fit, but the numerical correlation is only in the figure. The reported 15% reduction is derived from the left-panel fit.
rows.check: The measure is task failure rate against training-location count (diversity), not loss against parameters, tokens or compute. The value can be made more precise: the text gives the fitted exponent −0.229 from Fig. 10 (left), i.e. about 15% fewer failures per doubling. The r values appear only in the figure.

source_check.correct: For total training data fixed at 128 h, the text gives exponent −0.229 and approximately 15% fewer navigation failures per doubling of training locations. Numerical Pearson correlation is figure-only.
source_check.locator_found: Section IV-C, Figure 10 caption and following paragraphs, lines 487–513.
source_check.problem: The fit is not wholly figure-only: its exponent and implied failure reduction appear explicitly in the text.

rows.value: Figure only; the text reports a power-law relationship.

rows.check: Same construct mismatch as r1: failure rate against location count, with 16 h per location, so total data also grows. No fit coefficients appear in the text.

source_check.locator_found: Section IV-C, Figure 8 caption, Figure 10 caption and power-law discussion, lines 456–513.

rows.subject: MLP-BC policies trained on data subsets (aggregate trend)
rows.operation_detail: Increase the amount of data sampled from fixed sets of training locations.
rows.measure: Navigation success rate as training data per location increases
rows.value: The text says additional data from a fixed set of locations has negligible effect and that performance gain is already saturated at 2 h per location, below the quantities considered.
rows.note: The stated saturation qualifies the scaling result: the reported power law is for location diversity, not a general benefit from increasing data quantity.
rows.check: Success rate against hours per location at fixed location sets. The text calls the effect negligible and saturated at 2 h. This is a downstream robot metric, not loss, so it cannot bear on V5's loss power law.

rows.subject: MLP-BC policies trained with data from 8 locations
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate a training subset containing data from 8 locations.
rows.value: The text reports a dip in overall success rates; these policies got stuck in infinite spinning loops in Kisumu.
rows.note: The authors attribute the anomaly to unequal data quality across locations and say the dip is remedied when more locations are added.
rows.check: This is an anomaly note rather than a scaling measurement: a dip at 8 locations caused by spinning loops in Kisumu. It should be a caveat on r1/r2, not its own row.

source_check.correct: Policies trained on the particular 8-location subset entered infinite spinning loops in Kisumu, lowering aggregate success; adding further locations remedied the effect.
source_check.problem: Accurate qualitative caveat, but not an independent scaling measurement; it belongs with the location-scaling results.

relation.reason: The study trains and evaluates policies across controlled data subsets and fits their real-world failure rates to a power law. These own results test V6 rather than merely discussing scaling.

tranche.reason: V6 explicitly covers downstream performance improving predictably with scale. Section IV-C experimentally fits navigation failure against training-location count, including a condition where total data grows at 16 h per location. This is a result on that version in a new setting; V6 does not require language-model pretraining loss.

source_check.notes: State checks above use the supplied versions=none; r1/r2 need V6 links and condition-specific verdict review. The fixed-location saturation in r3 qualifies data-quantity scaling; no pretraining-loss or large-run extrapolation test is reported.
